title: Development of REGAI: Rubric Enabled Generative Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper proposes and evaluates REGAI (Rubric Enabled Generative Artificial Intelligence), a retrieval-augmented generation and large language model-based system designed to improve automated evaluation of unstructured text. The main problem addressed is that LLMs can produce plausible but inaccurate or inconsistent judgments, especially in high-stakes evaluation settings where human-like reasoning, consistency, and alignment with explicit criteria are required.

REGAI combines several components: a rubric that may be manually created or LLM-generated and then reviewed by a human expert; a scoring LLM that produces an initial numeric score and justification; a critiquing LLM that checks the score against the rubric and provides corrective feedback; and an iterative draft-critique-revision workflow. It also uses retrieval from a knowledge base of expert-created rubrics, grades, and critiques, with the goal of grounding outputs in prior human examples and strengthening performance over time. The paper explicitly discusses possible applications in academic grading, applicant screening, performance evaluation, client interaction assessment, proposal review, email prioritization, paper review, and transcript analysis.

Although the system is presented as broadly applicable, the only empirical evaluation reported uses the first 500 essays from the Hewlett Foundation Automated Essay Scoring dataset. In that experiment, REGAI is tested in two configurations: a single critique iteration versus a rubric-only approach. Results suggest that the critique cycle improves error reduction, weighted agreement, and score calibration relative to rubric-only scoring, but both approaches still fall short of human raters and show signs of overfitting due to a very small knowledge base. The paper concludes that REGAI is promising, but requires more robust knowledge bases, better prompt engineering, and additional validation across domains.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A rubric-enabled generative AI system built from large language models and retrieval-augmented generation to evaluate unstructured text using human-created or human-reviewed rubrics, iterative critique, and a growing knowledge base.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and preliminarily evaluates REGAI for automated essay scoring and discusses prospective use in academic grading; the system is also framed for rubric-based evaluation tasks more broadly.

findings.finding_summary: On the Hewlett Foundation Automated Essay Scoring Dataset (first 500 essays from essay set 8), the single-critique REGAI configuration showed better error and agreement metrics than the rubric-only approach, but not consistently better correlation. Reported overall metrics were Corr=0.49, MAE=4.37, and QWK=0.49 for single critique versus Corr=0.55, MAE=7.86, and QWK=0.26 for rubric-only; human raters were Corr=0.60, MAE=2.03, and QWK=0.59.
findings.measure: Automated essay scores compared with human-provided scores; correlation, mean absolute error, and quadratic-weighted kappa

quality_tier_rationale: This is a preliminary evaluation of a proposed system using one dataset and limited human-approved examples, not a rigorous experimental study. The paper also reports the results as indicative/proof-of-concept rather than definitive, with limited methodological detail.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences suggest the critique cycle may improve scoring accuracy and agreement, but the impact is mixed and the system remains below human raters. The effect is meaningful for the specific essay-scoring setting, but the paper does not report a single effect size and the evidence is early-stage.
